newsitem.title: USA: N.H. regulators order electric competition.
newsitem.headline: N.H. regulators order electric competition.

text.p: - The Public Utilities Commission of New Hampshire Friday issued an interim order that monopoly electric utilities break into separate generation and distribution companies by 1998.

The PUC will allow the state's largest utility, Public Service Co, to retain 80 percent of its stranded costs - investments in power plants and the like that were required under monopoly operation, but would not be viable in a competitive environment.

The commission said under its plan, customers will see a 19 percent rate cut. If this interim order takes effect, that would bring an average 500 kilowatt residential bill down to about $60 a month from its current average of $73.08.
Although there was no immediate response, Public Service has said it could challenge the decision in court and declare bankruptcy if it was financially injured.

The PUC allowed two regional utilities, Granite State Electric Co., a subsidiary of New England Electric Systems, and Unitil Corp to recover 100 percent of stranded costs because their electric rates were below regional averages.

"The Commission has established a strong foundation for retail competition and set interim stranded cost charges that are equitable, appropriate and balanced," said PUC Executive Director Thomas B. Getz. "Great care has been taken, moreover, to achieve the goal of near-term rate relief while preserving the financial integrity of the utilities, notably PSNH."

The commission ordered utilities to decide by the end of the year whether to become generation or distribution utilities. Distribution utilities will continue to be regulated by the commission. NEES has already said it wishes to go solely into distribution.

Generation utilities will be deregulated -- with the commission barring transactions among affiliated companies. This would mean that Public Service could no longer acquire power from its parent company, Northeast Utilities, even electricity from the Seabrook nuclear power plant.

The commission said the new plan could begin by Jan. 1, 1998. Industrial and commercial users would begin shopping for electricity by July 1. Residenial and small commercial customers could continue to receive service from their local distribution company under what is known as "default service" similar to present telephone deregulation.
